content.text:
Not autonomously, currently.

- The engine supports any entity drinking via `DrinkIntent` and the canonical `drinkSystem` ([drinkSystem.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/drinkSystem.js:11)).
- Monster AI currently picks up and uses certain scrolls, but there is no corresponding potion pickup/drinking behavior ([aiScrollSystem.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/aiScrollSystem.js:57), [scheduler.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/main/scheduler.js:227)).
- So a monster could drink if code explicitly gives it a `DrinkIntent` for an inventory potion, but ordinary monsters will not decide to drink potions on their own.
I wonder if it should be interuptable?

I’m checking how “drink” is modeled relative to other interruptible actions—especially whether potion drinking is currently instantaneous or already routed through the action/channeling runtime—so I can answer whether interruption fits the existing rules cleanly.

content.text: I mean it would really change the calculus

Exactly. It would turn potions into tactical commitments instead of invisible stat corrections.

An interruptible monster drink would create meaningful choices:

- Ignore the monster and let it recover.
- Spend damage to cancel the drink.
- Use stun, silence, knockback, or line-of-sight breaks as counters.
- Decide whether chasing the monster is worth giving it time to quaff.

That makes potion-carrying monsters feel much more readable and fair. I’d make drinking a visible one-turn commitment, but reserve it for intelligent or explicitly potion-using monsters so it becomes a deliberate archetype rather than universal AI behavior.
FYI: player *and* monster drink

Got it—then drinking should be a shared rule, not a monster-specific behavior.

If both players and monsters can drink, making the action interruptible would change the core potion calculus for everyone: potions become committed, telegraphed actions with counterplay. The clean design is one canonical drink wind-up for both actor types, with damage interrupting before consumption.

content.text:
Here’s the current potion landscape, grouped by what drinking them actually does.

### Immediate combat sustain

- Health Potion — heals 25% max HP.
- Potion of Radiance — heals, cleanses, and grants regeneration.
- Berserk Potion — restores stamina to full.
- Mana Potion — improves mana regeneration for 20 turns.
- Stamina Potion — restores stamina.
- Stamina Elixir — improves stamina regeneration.
- Potion of Speed — grants haste for 20–30 turns.

These are the most affected by interruption. They are emergency buttons today; with a drink wind-up, using one becomes a commitment and can be denied by damage.

### Defensive preparation

- Potion of Stoneskin — grants a strong armor buff.
- Fire Ward Potion — fire resistance for 40 turns.
- Poison Ward Potion — poison resistance for 40 turns.
- Lightning Ward Potion — lightning resistance.
- Acid Ward Potion — acid resistance.
- Anti-Venom — clears poison.
- Potion of Echoing Focus — grants keen vision and luck.
- Potion of Precision — improves critical chance.
- Mana Elixir — improves mana regeneration for 30 turns.

These are less “panic heal” and more pre-fight preparation. A wind-up makes sense and encourages drinking before entering danger rather than during combat.

### Harmful or risky when consumed

- Potion of Poison — applies poison.
- Potion of Sickness — damage plus poison.
- Potion of Paralysis — stuns/paralyzes the drinker.
- Potion of Hallucination — confusion-like effect.
- Potion of Blindness — blinds the drinker.
- Potion of Weakness — reduces health/stamina capacity.
- Potion of Sluggishness — reduces stamina regeneration.
- Potion of Confusion — confusion.
- Potion of Acid — direct acid damage and burning.
- Flask of Oil — causes burning.

These raise an important distinction: if drinking is interrupted before completion, the harmful potion should remain unconsumed. That makes accidental cursed/unknown potion use less punishing, but still preserves the risk once the drink completes.

### Utility and special cases

- Potion of Water — quenching, blessing, splashing.
- Vial of Holy Water — blessing and anti-flame utility.
- Potion of Radiance — also has special undead-facing behavior.
- Several potions can be thrown or applied to weapons instead of drunk.

The authored definitions are concentrated in [potions.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/potions.js:73), with additional potions in [potionEchoingFocus.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/potionEchoingFocus.js:3) and [potionOfRadiance.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/potionOfRadiance.js:10).

The main implication is that a single universal drink rule is surprisingly coherent:

- drinking takes a turn or more;
- the actor must remain still;
- damage/status interruption cancels it;
- nothing is consumed until completion;
- throwing and applying remain separate instant actions;
- drinking a harmful potion is also interruptible, but once completed its consequences are immediate.

I would avoid making drink time unique for every potion initially. Use one shared default—probably 1–2 turns—and only add per-potion timing when a specific potion’s fantasy or power clearly demands it.

Agreed. Potions remain fast, one-action quaffs. Food becomes the deliberate “sit down and eat” action.

There are 23 authored `food` items.

### Basic food and ingredients

- `food_ration` — Ration
- `food_iron_ration` — Iron Ration
- `food_wild_berries` — Wild Berries
- `food_wild_herbs` — Wild Herbs
- `food_raw_fish` — Raw Fish
- `food_golden_carp` — Golden Carp
- `food_moonfin` — Moonfin
- `food_wheat` — Wheat
- `food_carrot` — Carrot
- `food_corn` — Corn
- `food_mushrooms` — Dungeon Mushrooms

Most are marked as cooking ingredients, but they can currently be eaten directly.

### Prepared meals

- `food_stew` — Town Stew
- `food_hearty_stew` — Hearty Stew
- `food_trail_bread` — Trail Bread
- `food_mushroom_broth` — Mushroom Broth
- `food_ember_roast` — Ember Roast
- `food_spider_skewer` — Spider Skewer
- `food_hunter_hash` — Hunter Hash
- `food_grave_bisque` — Grave Bisque
- `food_fisher_supper` — Fisher’s Supper

These apply nutrition plus persistent buffs, so channeling makes particularly strong sense for them.

### Dungeon soups

- `food_pilgrim_stew` — Pilgrim’s Barley Stew
- `food_moonmilk_chowder` — Moonmilk Chowder
- `food_witchlight_broth` — Witchlight Broth

These are especially good candidates for a longer “sit and eat” action because they are bowls/meals with substantial ongoing effects ([dungeonSoups.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/dungeonSoups.js:13)).

The food catalog is in [economy.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/economy.js:55) and [dungeonSoups.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/dungeonSoups.js:13).

One important boundary: corpses are edible through a separate corpse-eating path, not as catalog items with `type: "food"`. That probably deserves its own timing rules rather than automatically inheriting meal-eating time.

The conceptual split now looks clean:

- Potion: quaff now; immediate effect; spends the action.
- Food: sit down; remain still; complete the eating channel; then receive nutrition and food effects.
- Corpse: monster-specific eating behavior, potentially faster, riskier, or restricted by anatomy.

okay great, lets take a spin on food broadly, food is an "over time" behavior from now on.

NOTE: I feel like corpse eating is really no dfferent -- maybe you can explain why we have two eating pathways.

I’ll trace the corpse-eating path alongside ordinary food use first. The likely question is whether “corpse” is a different mechanic or just a different food source with monster-specific effects; I’ll verify that before proposing the channel boundary.
